call.text: The passage makes pain tangible. The pulse of nausea gives his distress a physical rhythm. When his threat breaks off, we can hear the effort it costs him to speak. Liam’s quiet promise to take them home gives “brother” its weight, letting a single word carry the affection between them.

It would be in character for Hux to use the Knights’ fascination with the Force against them. He’d take particular satisfaction in fooling warriors who regard an ordinary officer with contempt. His betrayal of Kylo in The Rise of Skywalker also suggests a sharper motive than loyalty to the First Order. Hux would relish proving that he understands Kylo’s former followers better than Kylo does. The false holocron would be a clever ploy if the Knights had a specific reason to want it. They aren’t collectors of Jedi or Sith lore, so a mysterious relic alone is a thin lure. If they believed it held a secret Kylo had kept from them, their decision to investigate would follow from the split. Your question cuts off after “putting it on,” so the placement remains an open part of that judgment.

Under *Trump v. United States* (2024), a former President has absolute immunity from criminal prosecution for acts within his exclusive constitutional authority, at least presumptive immunity for other official acts, and no presidential immunity for unofficial acts. An indictment’s description of an act cannot settle its status. A court must examine the function the President performed. A private electoral effort cannot acquire immunity simply because the President pursued it through an official channel, and an allegation of corrupt motive cannot transform an official act into a private one.

The strongest originalist bridge to absolute immunity runs through the separation of powers. If the Constitution commits a decision exclusively to the President, Congress cannot use criminal law to dictate that decision. Consider a pardon. Even abundant evidence that a pardon was unwise would give Congress no power to punish the former President for granting it. The bridge to presumptive immunity is more contested. The Court reasoned that the prospect of later prosecution could distort decisions made in office. For an official act outside the exclusive core, the prosecution must show that applying the criminal prohibition poses no danger of intrusion on the authority and functions of the Executive Branch. The Court left open whether that presumption can ever be overcome.

There is also an originalist bridge to a narrower rule. The Constitution expressly protects legislators through the Speech or Debate Clause but supplies no comparable text for the President. Hamilton, in *Federalist No. 69*, distinguished the President from the British king partly through the President’s exposure to ordinary prosecution after removal. Article I likewise preserves criminal liability after an impeachment conviction. That clause establishes a bridge from conviction to prosecution, but its wording does not make conviction a prerequisite. The historical evidence for post-office accountability is more abundant than the evidence for any precise boundary around official acts. It would be too quick to transform that general evidence into a complete answer about a particular prosecution.

My originalist judgment is that exclusive presidential powers provide the firmest bridge to immunity. Outside that core, a narrower reading is persuasive: a former President may be prosecuted through a valid criminal statute unless its application would impair a constitutionally assigned function. The distinction matters most when there is abundant evidence of wrongdoing. A court cannot quickly resolve immunity through the strength of that evidence alone. Under binding precedent, it must first decide whether the alleged conduct falls outside presidential duties, within an area of shared authority, or within a power exercised through the President’s exclusive constitutional authority.

My Answer: In natal astrology, Chariklo symbolizes the ability to stay present with someone through uncertainty. Named for the mythic wife of Chiron, she brings attention to the person who sits beside the wounded healer. Her sign can suggest how you offer care, while her house can point to the part of life where others most often turn to you. My Conclusion: Chariklo asks you to notice the difference between care you give freely and care you feel obliged to give. Knowing your limits can make your support more dependable. Future Outlook: As your relationship with this part of your chart develops, you may grow more comfortable asking a simple question before stepping in: “Would you like help, or would you like me to stay with you?”

I sang to the echo asleep in the well,  
“One more little note till the bucket is full.”  
The echo sang back, “You can fill it with song,  
but ‘one more’ survives when the last note is gone.”

(Sing [softly {to the echo (of the echo [of this note])}].)  
One more, one more, let the melody climb.  
My mouth needs a breath, but the numbers have time.

Infinity means that however you count,  
you can always add one to the highest amount.  
I can grasp why that’s true, I can sing you the rule,  
though I can’t hear each note in that bottomless pool.

Does space carry on past the last star we see?  
The dark keeps that answer from you and from me.  
I wind up the bucket. The moon’s on the tin.  
“One more?” calls the echo. I draw breath again.

Blessed Founders, thirteen stars still crown thy thrones.  
Shall Washington’s standard grace these broken battlements?  
Grant starving thralls fresh bread!

Franklin’s thunder breaks princely chains.  
Shall freed thralls forgive crushing debts?  
Shield stricken hamlets from temptation’s snare!
